newsitem.title: USA: Raytheon ordered to pay $60 mln in damages.
newsitem.headline: Raytheon ordered to pay $60 mln in damages.

text.p: The families of two men killed in a 1991 air crash were awarded $60 million after a jury found the aircraft manufacturer failed to warn of potential defects, a lawyer for the plaintiffs said on Monday.

A federal jury Friday ordered Beech Aircraft, the plane's maker, and its Lexington, Massachusetts-based parent Raytheon Co., to pay $30 million each in compensatory damages to the families of Dr. Paul Dempsey and pilot Brian Smith, who both died in the March 27, 1991, crash.
The families had alleged the Beech Baron aircraft had a spinning tendency that caused the plane to enter unrecoverable flat spins.

The suit, filed in U.S. District Court in Arizona, said Beech failed to warn of the dangers of flat spins despite discussions with the Federal Aviation Administration and National Transportation Safety Board about uncontrollable flat spins.

Dempsey had bought a six-seat, twin-engine Baron 58P aircraft and hired Smith to assist him in familiarizing himself with the new plane. During a routine training maneuver the plane entered a flat spin and spun out of control.
"The FAA's inaction is another example of its tombstone mentality," John Howie, attorney for the family of Brian Smith, said in a statement.

"They take no action until the body count cries out for change. Hopefully, the FAA and Beech will now properly deal with this dangerous flat spin condition, the results of which have been characterized by NTSB documents as 'predictable and catastrophic'," Howie said.
Raytheon said on Monday it planned to appeal the verdict.

"The facts do not support the verdict and in a post-trial motion we will ask to set the verdict aside, which would result in a new trial," said Jim Gregory, a spokesman for Raytheon Aircraft Co. "The facts will ultimately support our case."
Beech Aircraft changed its name to Raytheon Aircraft Co. in 1994.
